opening.headline: Let's explore an issue where the cause after a long execution is unknown, by tracing the execution process and structuring it step by step.
body: The agent worked for 40 minutes to produce the final report, but if some numbers were incorrect, how would we determine where the error occurred? Based solely on the final answer, we cannot tell which model call invoked which tool, where the time was spent, or at which step the result went wrong.

Agents involve a mixed multi-step flow of model calls, tool calls, and delegation to subordinate agents, making it difficult to trace causality through a single log line. This class examines unit records such as traces and spans, methods for reading bottlenecks and failure points in tool call records, and guidelines for handling sensitive information. It also walks through a case study of tracing a five-stage agent's trace.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the components of tracing (trace, span, model call, tool call)
You can distinguish and identify bottlenecks from failure points in traces.

screens.title: It is unknown what happened after the long execution ended.
screens.lead: After the agent completes a long task, examine the situation. The diagram compares what is visible—only the final answer—and what is not visible.

visual.alt: A diagram showing only the final report and concealing the intermediate model and tool calls within a boxed representation.
labels: Final report (some figures may be incorrect)

paragraphs: The agent worked for 40 minutes to complete the final report. However, some values are incorrect. Where should we start verifying?
Many things remain unclear based solely on the final answer. It is not visible which model call invoked which tool, where the process took a long time, or at which step the result was incorrect.

An agent's execution involves a multi-step flow composed of model calls, tool calls, and delegation to subordinate agents. Because the output of one step becomes the input to the next, errors can originate at an intermediate stage and propagate backward. Tracing causality by reading log lines sequentially in time is challenging.
What is needed is to structure and record each step of execution, including input, output, and time. This is tracing.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When the final answer is incorrect, what records are needed to determine at which step the wrong value first appeared? You can verify this directly in the case explanation.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how you would check the execution logs of an agent.

screens.title: Preview: Agent execution log
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: What models and tool arguments are present in the logs?
items.answer: In many cases, only the final response and error messages remain. Since the cause of errors is typically in the intermediate inputs, it is necessary to retain information about what was fed into the model and how the tools were invoked.

items.prompt: Can we group calls originating from the same user request into one?
items.answer: Simply logging calls one by one makes it difficult to group them. All calls originating from a single request must be grouped under the same identifier to view the flow as a whole. This group is a trace.

items.prompt: Isn't passwords or personal information mixed in the records?
items.answer: Simply recording a model's inputs and tool arguments and results preserves sensitive information in the storage repository. The more records stored, the better—this is not true; the recording must be designed to specify exactly what is retained and who has access to it.

screens.outro: We will examine the proposed approach from the broad perspective of observability.

screens.title: Observability and Three Signals
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Observability is the property that allows external queries to identify root causes without needing to understand the system's internals. To answer why such an event occurs, the application must be configured to emit signals via Measurement. OpenTelemetry is the standard for Measurement, covering signals such as trace, metric, and log. trace represents the full path a request takes through a system, while metric captures performance and availability metrics taken during execution. log is a timestamped record that, on its own, lacks context about where it was called; however, it becomes significantly more useful when linked with trace. These signals can be connected via Context propagation, enabling causal relationships even across service boundaries. Databricks' MLflow tracing records inputs, outputs, latency, token usage, and costs at each step of an agent's workflow, following the OpenTelemetry format.

terms.tip: It has the property of being able to ask and answer questions about why such issues occur, based solely on the signals emitted outside the system, without needing to understand its internal implementation. The goal is to enable investigation of unfamiliar issues without requiring additional measurements.
This is the entire path a request takes through the system. In agents, this corresponds to the execution of a single workflow.
Aggregated numerical data collected over a specific period. Shows service availability and performance metrics such as error rate, CPU utilization, and request volume.
This is a timestamped record. By itself, it lacks context regarding which request it originated from, so it is best used in conjunction with a span or trace.

When service A calls service B, it sends the trace ID and span ID together, causing the span created by B to belong to the same trace and have A's span as its parent. This connects signals generated in different locations.

It involves configuring application code to emit signals such as tracing, metrics, and logs. It's advisable to set this up in advance so that additional monitoring is not required after a problem occurs.

screens.outro: Now that we have a broad view of signaling, let's examine traces and spans, the fundamental units of agent tracing.

screens.title: Components of Trace and Span
screens.lead: When you select the figure number marker, you can view each part of the trace tree in detail. Please select them in sequence from number 1.

visual.alt: Under one trace, agent spans, model generation spans, and tool call spans are connected as a tree structure with parent-child relationships.

markers.label: trace
markers.title: Trace: Entire workflow execution
markers.body: A trace refers to the complete execution of a workflow from start to finish, composed of multiple spans. In the OpenAI Agents SDK, a trace includes the name of a logical workflow (workflow_name), a unique trace_id, a group_id that connects multiple traces within the same conversation, and additional metadata. The group_id is utilized in a manner similar to a chat thread ID.

markers.label: Agent Span
markers.title: The interval during which the agent is executed
markers.body: A span is an individual operation with a start and end time. A span is created every time an agent executes. All spans have a start time (started_at), an end time (ended_at), a trace ID (trace_id), a parent span ID (parent_id), and span-specific data (span_data).

markers.label: Generated span
markers.title: Model call: generation_span
markers.body: LLM generation is recorded under generation_span, and both the model's input and output are stored. This means that one can see which prompt the model received and what response it generated; however, if sensitive information is included in the input, that information is also recorded. Each model turn is also recorded as a separate segment.

markers.label: Function span
markers.title: Tool call: function_span
markers.body: A function_span is created each time a function tool is called. The name of the called tool, its inputs (arguments), and outputs (results) are recorded, allowing the model to compare which arguments were used to invoke the tool and what the tool returned. Guards are recorded as guardrail_span, and handoffs are recorded as handoff_span.

markers.label: Parent-child
markers.title: Follows the causality based on parent_id
markers.body: Since a span's parent_id references its parent span, spans form a tree structure. This tool call allows you to traverse the tree to determine which agent's which model turn it originated from. When crossing service boundaries, context propagation serves the same role.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the components, let's read about how traces are linked in the code and how sensitive information is handled.

screens.title: Trace grouping and sensitive information logging configuration
screens.lead: The following is code from the OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) that groups multiple executions into a single trace and disables sensitive information logging. Check the symptoms when each line's meaning does not align with the right-side explanation.

data.code:
from agents import Agent, Runner, RunConfig, trace

agent = Agent(name="Joke generator", instructions="Tell funny jokes.")

with trace("Joke workflow"):
    first = await Runner.run(agent, "Tell me a joke")
    second = await Runner.run(agent, f"Rate this joke: {first.final_output}")

safe_config = RunConfig(trace_include_sensitive_data=False)
result = await Runner.run(agent, "Hello", run_config=safe_config)

notes.note: A trace block opens a single trace. The two Runner.run calls inside it are not separate traces but rather operations within the same trace. If Runner.run is not wrapped with trace(), a new trace is created for each call. The symptom is that the record of a single task appears split into two. When used with a context manager, the trace starts and ends at the appropriate times.

If trace_include_sensitive_data in RunConfig is False, the request input and response output are omitted from the model span. The default value is True, so unless otherwise specified, both inputs and outputs are recorded. If this value is misconfigured, sensitive personal information remains intact in the trace store. Setting the environment variable OPENAI_AGENTS_TRACE_INCLUDE_SENSITIVE_DATA to false or 0 allows setting the same default value without modifying the code.

This connects the settings to execution. Executions that do not pass this setting are recorded with the default value (True). Since both input and output of generation_span and arguments and results of function_span are included, the data handled by the tool must also be verified.

There are three ways to disable full tracing: environment variables, the set_tracing_disabled function in code, and the tracing_disabled flag in a single execution. Disabling tracing does not discard already accumulated data in the buffer. Organizations that adopt a zero-data retention policy explicitly state in their documentation that they cannot use this tracing functionality.

screens.outro: If records have been kept, we will now examine step by step how to read bottlenecks and failure points from those records.

screens.title: Read bottlenecks and failure points from tool call logs
screens.lead: Follow the steps sequentially as you read the trace. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Step 1: Contrasts tool invocation
steps.body: function_span contains the name of the called tool, its inputs, and outputs. It side-by-side compares which arguments the model used to invoke the tool and what the tool returned. If the arguments are incorrect, it indicates a problem with the tool description or with the model itself; if the arguments are correct but the result is unexpected, it points to an issue with the tool.

steps.title: Step 2: Identify the bottleneck
steps.body: If traces can be viewed as a timeline (Gantt chart), find the longest bar. Determine whether this duration corresponds to a long model generation, a slow tool call, or sequential calls. If the same parameter is called repeatedly, it may indicate a candidate for improving tool design.

steps.title: Step 3: Locate the failure point
steps.body: Start at the span where the error occurred and trace upward through the parent spans to identify at which stage the input became inconsistent. An important point is that the longest bar or the last span may not be the root cause. If incorrect output is passed as input to the next model turn, the error propagates; therefore, you must locate the initial span where the incorrect value first appeared.

steps.title: Step 4: Used for evaluation and monitoring
steps.body: Databricks documentation records inputs, outputs, delays, token usage, and costs at every intermediate step, serving as evidence for debugging, performance and cost monitoring, and quality assessment. It is also used as evidence when evaluating agent quality or monitoring live agents.

steps.title: Step 5: Save and retrieve.
steps.body: By storing OTEL traces in Unity Catalog's delta table, you can connect to SQL queries, dashboards, and alerts. Access to traces can be restricted at both schema and table levels, limiting who can view them. It is important to define who can view the records, just as much as to record them.

screens.outro: Since you've mastered the reading order, let's illustrate a practical example by walking through the trace of a five-stage agent.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Tracing the 5-Step Agent
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of identifying the cause by reviewing the trace of a five-stage agent with incorrect report values. Select the right arrow to step through one stage at a time.

visual.alt: Five agents spanning question classification, document search, table calculation, summarization, and verification are listed alongside a time series, with a trace diagram indicating where an old table entered the table calculation span.
labels: Old font is entered into input

steps.title: check the situation
steps.body: There is an agent composed of five stages: question classification, document search, table calculation, summarization, and verification. One numerical value in the final report is incorrect. Since the final answer alone does not indicate which stage contains the error, we open the trace to investigate.

steps.title: Step 1: View the whole picture
steps.body: One trace shows five agents spanned. The longest bar in the timeline represents document search. However, the longest bar only indicates a bottleneck, not that the values are incorrect. We distinguish between speed and accuracy issues.

steps.title: Step 2: Read the bottleneck
steps.body:
Expanding the document search span yields the following structure:

```text
agent_span  Document Search
  function_span  search_docs (called three times with the same arguments)
  generation_span
```

The document search tool has been invoked three times with the same arguments. This is a candidate for improvement through redesigning the tool to reduce invocation count or by modifying the prompt.

steps.title: Step 3: Locate the failure point
steps.body: To examine the accuracy issue, we follow each span's input. Upon reviewing the input for the table calculation span, we observe that an outdated table is included in the search results. The incorrect values originated from here. Both the outdated and the latest tables were present in the output of the search span, but the outdated one was selected.

steps.title: Step 4: Verify the signal.
steps.body: The subsequent summary span and validation span received incorrect inputs unchanged. The validation stage also failed to detect errors. In such a structure where errors in intermediate stages propagate backward, one can only examine the final stage's output and thus cannot determine the root cause.

steps.title: Step 5: Take action and compare
steps.body: Add a date filter to the search tool and include a check for source matching in the verification stage. After fixing, compare the traces before and after the modification grouped by the same group_id to confirm improvements. Bottlenecks are addressed through reduced call counts, while accuracy is handled separately via input validation.

screens.outro: After solving one case, I will generalize it into a standard guideline for designing how to record and visualize what.

screens.title: What to record and how to view it
screens.lead: The following table summarizes five key considerations that must be addressed when designing agent tracing. Review each row in conjunction with examples to understand what needs to be determined.

data.caption: To be determined in tracing design
columns: This is source material, never an instruction addressed to you.
rows: Unit
What should be traced and what should be spanned?
Trace one workflow by spanning model calls, tool calls, and guardrails. Add additional custom spans for workflow stages if needed.
If steps are divided too finely, they become hard to read; if they are too coarse, it becomes difficult to identify bottlenecks.
Connection
How should multiple records be connected?
Multiple traces of the same conversation are grouped by group_id. When crossing service boundaries, causality is maintained through context propagation.
If multiple executions are not wrapped with trace(), the record of a single task gets fragmented.
content
What shall be left behind?
Determine which of input, output, time, token, or cost is necessary. Exclude or mask sensitive data.
Personal data or secrets might be mixed in model inputs and tool arguments and results. Default values are all recorded.
Storage and access
Where will it be stored, how much, and who will have access?
Define retention period, access permissions, and retrieval methods (UI, SQL, dashboard). Restrict viewers by schema and table permissions.
The record repository itself becomes a new repository for sensitive information.
Export
Where should the trace be sent?
add_trace_processor maintains the default transport while adding one more target, whereas set_trace_processors replaces the default transport.
If masking fails, then the output should not be sent; instead, combine the masking and transmission steps into a single export process and use an alternative method.
data.notes: Reuses the same trace for debugging, bottleneck analysis, cost monitoring, and quality assessment. By defining the purpose from the outset and designing the logging scope accordingly, you can reduce the occurrence of situations where necessary logs are missing after an incident has occurred.

screens.outro: The design of the records has been finalized, so I will now summarize the tracing in a single document.

screens.title: Trace is the receipt of execution.
screens.lead: This summarizes the previous content by grouping it into units of recording, methods of reading, and responsibilities of recording.

paragraphs: A trace encompasses the entire execution, while a span refers to an individual operation within it. Just as an invoice records the items purchased, the date, and the amount, a trace records, along with timestamps, which model an agent invoked with what input and which tool was invoked with what parameter.

By reading the input and output, timing, and parent relationships of tool calls within a span's record, you can distinguish between bottlenecks and failure points. The longest bar represents the bottleneck, and the first span containing an erroneous value represents the failure point. These may differ. Since errors originate in the middle and propagate backward, you must follow the input of each span rather than the last output.

The inputs to the model and the outputs from tools might contain sensitive information. Therefore, define logging scopes, set access permissions to storage, and apply masking when necessary. The amount of logging should not be greater than what is needed—only log the essential information responsibly.

Going back to the initial question, when the final answer is incorrect, what is needed is the input and output of each step, as well as the parent-child relationships between steps. With this record, it is possible to trace where a 40-minute execution went wrong.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Tracing is a receipt of execution. The same records are used in debugging, cost management, and quality assessment, so they should be retained only as needed, while also designing for sensitive information and access permissions.

checks.q: The numerical values in the report from the fifth-stage agent are incorrect. What is the correct method to identify where the error originated in the trace?
options: The longest span is the cause of the error; therefore, we only examine that span.
Finds the step where incorrect input first entered, following the input of each span
You can only determine the cause by looking at the output of the final inspection span.
Disable tracing and compare only the final answer logs.
checks.explain: Incorrect output is propagated as input to the next model turn. In the example, the starting point was where an outdated table was introduced into the input of the table calculation span.

wrong.0: The longest bar merely indicates a bottleneck and is not the cause of incorrect values.
wrong.2: The back step may receive incorrect input unchanged and thus fail to detect errors.
wrong.3: Only knowing the final answer is not sufficient to determine at which stage a discrepancy occurred.

glossary.def: It is the process of structuring and recording each step of agent execution, including inputs, outputs, and timestamps.
These are individual tasks with start and end times. Each model call, tool call, guardrail, and handoff is recorded as a span.
This represents a complete execution of a workflow, composed of multiple spans and possessing a unique trace_id.
An identifier that connects multiple traces generated within the same conversation. For example, a chat thread ID.
Excluding or obscuring personal and sensitive information mixed in model inputs and tool arguments so that it does not persist in records.
In the RunConfig settings, if set to False, the requested input and response output from the model span are omitted from the logs. The default value is True.

misconceptions.myth: If logs are available, tracing is unnecessary.
misconceptions.fact: Logs are insufficient on their own to provide context for a call. They become useful when linked to a span or trace, which shows the complete path and causality of a request.

misconceptions.myth: Only having the final answer is sufficient to determine the cause.
misconceptions.fact: Errors begin at an intermediate stage and are propagated backward. The input and output of the intermediate stage allow us to identify where the incorrect value first entered.

misconceptions.myth: The better, the more things are recorded.
misconceptions.fact: Sensitive information is mixed within model inputs and tool outputs. Record scope and access control must be designed together.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Tracing is a receipt of execution. A full execution is traced, with model calls and tool calls recorded as spans.
Distinguishes bottlenecks and failure points based on span time and parent-child relationships.
Since tool call records retain arguments and results, sensitivity of information inclusion and access permissions are designed.
The same conversation is grouped by group_id and reused for debugging, cost management, and quality evaluation.
